item.title: PCE Inflation Holds at 3.3% Ahead of Fed Chair Warsh's First Jackson Hole Speech
item.body:
## A Data Point With Unusually High Stakes

Wednesday's release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index — the inflation gauge the Federal Reserve says it watches most closely — landed with unusually high stakes attached. Core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, came in at 3.3% on a year-over-year basis, matching the prior month's pace rather than accelerating or cooling meaningfully.

The timing is what turned an otherwise routine data release into a market-moving event. Two days later, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is scheduled to deliver his first keynote address at the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole Economic Symposium since taking the helm of the central bank — a venue that recent Fed chairs have used to signal major shifts in policy thinking. Investors were always going to parse that speech line by line. Now they have a fresh inflation print to measure it against.

## What The Report Actually Showed

According to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis, headline PCE inflation and the core reading both remained above the Fed's long-standing 2% target. A few points stood out to economists reviewing the release:

- **Core PCE held steady** at 3.3% year-over-year, suggesting underlying price pressure has plateaued rather than resumed climbing — but also has not resumed its earlier descent toward target.
- **Personal income and spending** figures released alongside the price data pointed to a consumer that is still spending, though at a more measured pace than earlier in the cycle.
- **Services inflation**, which has been the stickiest component of the basket in recent years, appears to be the primary reason the overall figure has stalled rather than fallen further.

None of this amounts to a dramatic surprise in either direction. That, in itself, is the story: a "3.3% and steady" print gives policymakers no clean excuse to declare victory over inflation, but also no fresh alarm bell to justify holding rates higher for longer.

## Why Markets Are Fixated on September

Futures markets have spent recent weeks pricing in a meaningful probability that the Fed cuts its benchmark rate at the September meeting. A print like this one — neither hot enough to derail that expectation nor cool enough to cement it — tends to keep traders exactly where they were before the data dropped: leaning toward a cut, but not fully committed.

That ambiguity is precisely why Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks carry extra weight this year. A debut keynote from a new Fed chair is typically read as a signal-setting moment regardless of circumstance. Coming just 48 hours after an inflation report that resolved nothing, it becomes the tie-breaker markets are waiting on. Analysts caution that a single speech rarely commits a data-dependent Fed to a specific decision weeks in advance, but the framing, tone, and emphasis Warsh chooses — on labor market slack, on services inflation, on the risks of moving too early versus too late — will likely shape how confidently traders position ahead of the September Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

## The Balancing Act Facing a New Chair

Any incoming Fed chair inherits a communication challenge: markets look for continuity with prior policy frameworks while also watching for hints of a distinct approach. That challenge is sharper when the first major public address follows an inflation report that essentially punts the hardest questions.

Fed watchers will likely be listening for a few specific signals in the speech itself:

1. **Language around "sufficiently restrictive"** policy — whether Warsh characterizes current rates as still needed to cool the economy or as increasingly ready to ease.
2. **Emphasis on the labor market** relative to inflation — a pivot toward employment risks is often read as more dovish.
3. **Any reference to the "last mile" problem** — the well-documented pattern of inflation cooling quickly from very high levels but stalling before reaching target.

## What Comes Next

Between now and the September FOMC decision, additional employment and inflation data will arrive and could shift the calculus further in either direction — a reminder that a single PCE report or a single speech rarely tells the whole story. Markets tend to treat Jackson Hole remarks as directional guidance rather than a binding pre-commitment, and Fed officials have historically preserved optionality until the meeting itself.

For now, the takeaway from Wednesday's data is narrower than headlines might suggest: inflation is not accelerating, but it is not resuming its decline either. That leaves the September decision genuinely open — and puts real weight on how Chair Warsh chooses to frame the path forward when he steps to the podium at Jackson Hole.
